section.title: The Folly of Trusting in Riches
section.sectionRationale: A wisdom psalm of the sons of Korah, cast as a riddle set to music and addressed to all peoples, not Israel alone. It argues that no amount of wealth can ransom a single soul from death, then breaks, at its very center, into a flash of hope that God Himself will provide the redemption no man can afford.
section.thesis: Wealth cannot ransom a single soul from death, so trusting in riches or envying those who have them is folly; yet God will redeem the life of His own from Sheol, a hope that looks forward to the greater redemption purchased by Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the riddle's call to all humanity; the folly of trusting wealth to buy off death; the flash of hope at the center, God will redeem my life from Sheol; and the closing refrain repeated for emphasis.

verses.text: Hear this, all you peoples; listen, all inhabitants of the world,
both low and high, rich and poor alike.
My mouth will impart wisdom, and the meditation of my heart will bring understanding.
I will incline my ear to a proverb; I will express my riddle with the harp:

units.label: No man can redeem his brother
units.note: the folly of trusting riches to buy off death

verses.text: Why should I fear in times of trouble, when wicked usurpers surround me?
They trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches.
No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God.
For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice,
that he should live on forever and not see decay.

For it is clear that wise men die, and the foolish and the senseless both perish 
and leave their wealth to others.

Their graves are their eternal homes, their dwellings for endless generations, 
even though their lands were their namesakes.
But a man, despite his wealth, cannot endure; he is like the {{behemah|beasts}} that perish.
This is the fate of the self-confident and their followers who endorse their sayings. Selah

units.label: God will redeem my life from Sheol
units.note: the flash of hope at the psalm's center

verses.text:
Like sheep they are destined for {{sheol|Sheol}}. Death will be their shepherd. The upright will rule them in the morning, and their form will decay in Sheol, 
far from their lofty abode.
But God will {{padah|redeem}} my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself. Selah
Do not be amazed when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases.
For when he dies, he will carry nothing away; his abundance will not follow him down.
Though in his lifetime he blesses his soul, and men praise you when you prosper,
he will join the generation of his fathers, who will never see the light of day.
A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish.

behemah.gloss: Beast, animal. The refrain that brackets the psalm, verses 12 and 20, says a man without understanding, however rich, is no better off in the end than a beast that perishes; wealth cannot change his fundamental mortality.

sheol.gloss: The realm of the dead, the grave. The wicked, trusting riches, are destined for Sheol with death itself as their shepherd; the psalm's turn is that God can reach into Sheol and redeem His own from it.

padah.gloss: To redeem, to ransom, to buy back at a price. No man can padah his brother from death, verse 7, but the psalmist confesses that God Himself will padah his life from Sheol, verse 15, a redemption only God can accomplish.

basic.context: This wisdom psalm is addressed to everyone, low and high, rich and poor, not just Israel. Its riddle is simple but devastating: no amount of money can buy back a single life from death. The wise die just like fools; the rich carry nothing into the grave. Right at the center of the psalm, though, comes a flash of hope that changes everything: God Himself will redeem the psalmist's life from Sheol, the realm of the dead, and take him to Himself.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm is a proverb set to music, meant to be pondered rather than merely admired. Its refrain, a man in his pomp without understanding is like the beasts that perish, brackets the whole argument and drives the point home: trusting riches, or envying those who have them, is folly in light of death. Verse 15 stands as the psalm's hinge, moving from universal helplessness to personal hope.
basic.originalLanguages: The wicked, trusting wealth, are destined for sheol, the grave, with death itself pictured as their shepherd. No man can padah, redeem or ransom, another from death; the price is simply too costly. Yet the psalmist confesses that God will padah his own life from Sheol, using the same word that elsewhere describes God's costly, decisive acts of rescue.
basic.typology: The impossible ransom no man can pay for another's soul, verses 7 to 9, anticipates Christ, who alone gives His life as a ransom for many. The confidence that God will take the psalmist to Himself out of Sheol anticipates the resurrection hope secured fully in Christ's own rising from the dead.
basic.christ: Verses 7 to 9 state plainly that no man can redeem his brother or pay God the price for a life. Jesus is the sole exception and fulfillment: He gives His life as a ransom for many, Mark 10:45, succeeding where every mere man fails. And where the wicked in this psalm are shepherded by death into Sheol, the psalmist's hope that God will take him to Himself is answered fully in the bodily resurrection Christ has secured for all who trust Him.
basic.god: God is shown as the only one who can ransom a life from death, a redemption beyond any human wealth or power. He is not impressed by riches or intimidated by the rich oppressor; His verdict on every life, however grand its house, is the same, and His mercy toward His own is greater than the grave.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 10:45 shows Jesus giving His life as the ransom no mere man could pay. Job 19:25 to 27 voices a kindred confidence that a Redeemer lives and will be seen even after death. 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 26 shows Christ's resurrection guaranteeing that death itself will finally be destroyed.
basic.oneStory: This wisdom psalm exposes the folly of trusting riches against death, then breaks into hope: God will redeem what money cannot. That hope runs forward to Jesus Christ, the one true ransom, whose resurrection guarantees that everyone God redeems will be taken to Himself beyond the reach of Sheol.

context.literary:
The psalm is a lesson delivered as a performance. It opens with a long summons, verses 1 to 4, that piles up audiences: all peoples, all inhabitants of the world, low and high, rich and poor. Then comes the singer's claim to speak wisdom, and the odd detail that he will express his riddle 'with the harp.' The teacher sings his sermon.

The body has two strophes, verses 5 to 12 and verses 13 to 20, and a refrain closes each: in verse 12 and again in verse 20 the man of wealth is 'like the beasts that perish.' The two refrains are not identical, and the difference is the key to the poem. In verse 12 the Hebrew says the man in his pomp does not 'lodge' or 'stay the night,' in the sense that he cannot remain. In verse 20 it says he does not 'understand.' The BSB has 'cannot endure' and 'without understanding.' The change of one letter turns an observation about his fate into a verdict on his folly. The rich man cannot last because he does not see that he cannot last.

The centre of the poem is the short verse 15, which stands between the long descriptions of death in verse 14 and the second warning in verse 16. It starts with a small word, 'But,' and its verb repeats the verb of verse 7 with a different subject. The man cannot redeem; God will. Verse 17 then answers verse 15 with another repeated verb: God will 'take' the psalmist, while the rich man will 'take' nothing away when he dies. Both are the same Hebrew verb.

The structure is a pair of arguments with a hope in the hinge. The first half puts the problem: no ransom can be paid. The second half draws the moral: do not be amazed at another man's wealth. Between them, like a door opening in a wall, God takes the psalmist to Himself. The heading names the sons of Korah, and the psalm belongs with the wisdom-flavoured songs of Book II.
context.historical:
The psalm speaks to an old and perennial situation, the one Psalm 73 also faces: the prosperous seem to get away with it, and the faithful poor are tempted to envy them or to fear them. Verse 5 says the psalmist is surrounded by trouble in evil days, and the Hebrew is difficult, since it literally speaks of 'the iniquity of my heels.' Some translators take this to mean the malice of those who trip him up, or the sins that dog his steps, and the BSB gives 'wicked usurpers.' Whichever it means, the singer knows what it is to feel hemmed in by people who have money and use it.

In Israel's world, wealth was more than comfort. It bought land, and land was the family's standing before God and the community. Verse 11 mentions men who name lands after themselves, which is the ancient way of leaving a memorial. The psalm rebukes that ambition. The footnote to verse 11 tells us that the Hebrew text reads 'their inward thoughts' where the Greek, Syriac and Aramaic translations read 'their graves,' so the ancient translators saw the same contrast: they think their houses are forever, and their true forever home is the grave.

The practice of ransom is behind verses 7 and 8. In Israelite law a life could sometimes be redeemed by payment. If an ox owner was liable for a death, he might be allowed to pay the price demanded and so redeem his life, Exodus 21:30, and every man numbered in the census paid a ransom for his life to the LORD, Exodus 30:12. Money could stand in for a life in certain cases. The psalm draws a line: no payment can buy off death itself.

Sheol, the place of the dead, was understood as a shadowy destination for every human being. Israel's neighbours built great tombs and stocked them with goods for the journey. The psalm's picture is the reverse: whatever the rich man built and bought stays behind, verse 17.
context.canonical:
Psalm 49 speaks with the voice of the wisdom writers. Its sentence about wealth and death is close to Ecclesiastes, which says that as a man came from his mother's womb, so he will depart, naked as he arrived, taking nothing for his labor, Ecclesiastes 5:15. Psalm 39:6 also says a man heaps up riches not knowing who will haul them away, and Psalm 62:10 says that if riches increase, do not set the heart on them. Job's friend and Job himself argued over whether the wicked prosper, Job 21:7-13, and Job 27:19 says the rich man lies down wealthy but will do so no more.

The question of why the wicked prosper is one Psalm 73 answers in a way that resembles Psalm 49. There the psalmist envied the arrogant, Psalms 73:3, until he entered God's sanctuary and discerned their end, Psalms 73:17. He then confesses that God will 'later receive me in glory,' Psalms 73:24, and in the Hebrew the verb is the same one used in Psalm 49:15.

Verse 15 is one of the Old Testament's boldest statements of hope past death, along with Psalm 16:10-11, where God will not abandon the soul to Sheol, and Job 19:25-27. In Genesis 5:24 Enoch is 'taken' by God, and Elijah is taken up in 2 Kings 2. Hosea 13:14 has the same phrase for God's rescue from the power of Sheol, and Paul uses that passage's taunt against death in 1 Corinthians 15:55.

The New Testament makes the psalm's two halves famous. Jesus told the parable of the rich fool, whose life was required of him that very night, Luke 12:16-21, and He asked what a man could give in exchange for his soul, Matthew 16:26. Paul warns that those who want to be rich fall into ruin, and that we brought nothing into the world and cannot take anything out, 1 Timothy 6:7-10. And the ransom of verse 7 is finally paid: Jesus gave His life as a ransom for many, Mark 10:45, and believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist has two aims and he holds them together. The first is to free his hearers from fear. Verse 5 asks, 'Why should I fear in times of trouble?' The people he addresses are surrounded by rich and powerful men who mock the faithful, and the way he helps them is not by promising that these men will be punished soon but by pointing out something everyone can see: they die. Their houses, their lands and their names cannot travel with them. To fear a man whose power ends at the grave is to give him more than he has.

The second aim is to free them from envy. Verse 16 tells them, 'Do not be amazed when a man grows rich.' The instinct to admire is met with a reminder. The person who is praised in his lifetime, verse 18, will join his fathers, and none of the praise goes with him. The psalm treats envy as a mistake of perspective, a failure to reckon with the end.

Behind both aims stands a more positive purpose. The teacher wants his hearers to see who the true redeemer is. The bleak truth of verses 7 and 8, that no man can redeem another, is meant to make the promise of verse 15 shine. The psalm does not leave the reader with only a warning, because it plants a hope. It teaches the listener to put trust in the God who can pay what no one else can, and to be content, since the one who has God has what wealth cannot buy.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes how rich and poor alike die, and how the wealthy behave. It does not command anyone to be poor, and it does not condemn possessions as such. The problem in view is trust in wealth and pride in it, verse 6, and 'riches without understanding,' verse 20. The New Testament keeps the same distinction when Paul tells those who are rich in this present age not to be arrogant or to put their hope in wealth, but to be rich in good works, 1 Timothy 6:17-19.

What it prescribes is a way of looking. Do not fear the man who is rich and cruel, do not envy the man who is rich and admired, and do not trust your own money to save you. The psalm is also a comfort to those who are poor, since the thing they lack cannot buy what matters. It is not a promise that believers will be richer than others, and it does not say the wicked always die dramatically. Verse 15 is a promise about God's own care of the faithful, and every reader is invited to make it their own.

debates.question: Does verse 15 teach a hope of resurrection beyond the grave, or simply rescue from present danger?

views.label: A confession of hope beyond the grave
views.case: The phrase 'He will surely take me to Himself' uses language reminiscent of Enoch's translation in Genesis 5:24, suggesting confidence in being received into God's presence beyond death itself, not merely rescued from a present threat.

views.label: A confidence of rescue from premature or violent death in this life
views.case: Sheol language elsewhere in the Psalms can describe the danger of dying prematurely or violently rather than a settled doctrine of resurrection, which Scripture reveals progressively and more fully in later books.

debates.bearing: Either reading affirms the psalm's central claim: God's redeeming reach extends further than any human ransom could go, a hope the New Testament shows fulfilled completely in the bodily resurrection secured by Christ.

debates.question: What does it mean that the rich man is 'like the beasts that perish,' verses 12 and 20?

views.label: He ceases to exist, as an animal does
views.case: Read plainly, the verse says that a man without understanding ends as the animals end, and some take that to mean total extinction of the foolish. Verse 19 says he will join his fathers, who 'will never see the light of day,' which can be heard as permanent darkness.

views.label: He shares the animal's mortality but not necessarily its end
views.case: The comparison is about what wealth cannot change: like the beasts, the rich die, and their status does not distinguish them. It is the same point Ecclesiastes 3:19-20 makes about everyone's common return to dust. The verdict is aimed at the man 'without understanding,' who forgets that he is dust. It does not say what awaits him afterward, and the contrast with the psalmist in verse 15 leaves a different destiny open.

views.label: He is like a beast in that death is his shepherd
views.case: Verse 14 pictures the wicked as sheep with Death as their shepherd, driving them into Sheol. On this view the image is of a helpless flock led by an owner who does not care for them. The focus is on helplessness, not on annihilation, and the contrast is with the LORD, who is the shepherd of His own, Psalms 23:1.

debates.bearing: The psalm's main point is unaffected: wealth gives no advantage before death. Whether it implies extinction or merely mortality, the New Testament frames the destiny beyond death in terms of resurrection to life or to judgment, John 5:28-29, and this psalm is not the place to settle it.

debates.question: What is meant by 'the upright will rule them in the morning,' verse 14?

views.label: A reversal at the day of God's judgment
views.case: Morning in the Psalms is when God acts to save, as in Psalms 46:5. The upright rule when the night of oppression ends. Read this way, the rich who ruled the poor are made subject in the reversal that the psalm expects.

views.label: A reversal within this life
views.case: The upright may see their oppressors fall in their lifetime, as the psalmists often hope. The 'morning' is then a turn of events in history.

views.label: An obscure line in a hard verse
views.case: The Hebrew of verse 14 is among the most difficult in the Psalter, especially the last clause about the form and the 'lofty abode.' Interpreters differ on its details, so it is wise to build on the clearer verses around it, 7 to 9 and 15.

debates.bearing: The difficulty of the verse does not affect the flow of the psalm, since the clear statements of verses 7 to 9 and 15 carry the argument.

study.originalLanguages:
The psalm opens with words for wisdom that are unusual in a song. Verse 3 speaks of 'wisdom,' chokhmot, in a plural form, a fullness of wisdom, and of 'understanding,' tevunot, also plural, from the root for discernment. The vocabulary belongs to the book of Proverbs, and verse 4 uses two of its terms for the sage's craft: mashal, 'proverb,' and chidah, 'riddle.' Proverbs 1:6 speaks of understanding 'the proverbs and parables, the sayings and riddles of the wise.' The psalmist claims a seat with the wise, and he puts his teaching to the harp, which shows that wisdom was sung.

The address in verse 2 has two pairs of contrasts. 'Both low and high' is literally 'sons of Adam' and 'sons of man,' where the first names the common run of humanity and the second people of rank. Then 'rich and poor,' 'ashir and evyon. The point is that no one is excluded from this lesson, because death makes no such distinctions.

The center of the psalm is a set of verbs for buying back. Verse 7 says 'No man can possibly redeem,' and the Hebrew doubles the verb, padoh lo yifdeh, using the same emphatic construction of an infinitive beside a finite verb. It is a strong denial: redeeming, he cannot redeem. The verb is padah, to ransom, to pay the price that sets someone free. It is next to 'ransom' in the same verse, kofer, the payment that covers a life. Exodus 30:12 uses kofer for the ransom each man paid at the census, and Exodus 21:30 uses the related word pidyon for the price by which a man might redeem his life. Verse 8 uses pidyon for the 'redemption of his soul,' calls it yaqar, costly or precious, and says it 'ceases' forever, so that payment must be stopped. No sum is enough.

The answer in verse 15 uses the same verb. 'God will redeem my life,' Elohim yifdeh nafshi, with the word 'nefesh' for the self. The very verb whose negation ran through verses 7 and 8 now has God as its subject. Then comes 'from Sheol,' and the phrase is literally 'from the hand of Sheol,' miyyad sheol, which is what Hosea 13:14 also says: 'I will ransom them from the power of Sheol.' The hand pictures Sheol as a grasping power, and God's redeeming is a rescue from its grip.

The second half of verse 15 says 'for He will surely take me,' ki yiqqachani, from laqach, to take. The same verb describes God taking Enoch in Genesis 5:24, and it occurs in the ask of Psalm 73:24, 'later receive me in glory.' It is the ordinary word for taking, but in these contexts God is the subject and a person the object, and the taking goes to God's presence. Verse 17 then says the rich man, when he dies, will not 'take' anything, using the same verb. God takes the psalmist, and the rich man takes nothing.

The word 'decay' in verse 9 is shachat, from the same word used in Psalms 16:10, 'nor will You let Your Holy One see decay.' Both verses use the verb 'see' with shachat, and the New Testament quotes the second in Acts 2:27 and 13:35. Finally, 'Sheol,' verse 14, is the realm of the dead. It is used as a place name, and here Death himself is pictured as the shepherd who leads the flock down.

typology.type: The ransom that no man can pay, verses 7 to 9
typology.fulfillment: The psalm stands at the impossible door: no one can pay God the price for another's life. Israel knew of ransom, from the census payment of Exodus 30:12 to the redeeming of the firstborn, but the psalm says death is beyond any silver. Jesus states the answer: the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. Peter says we were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19. Hebrews adds that He secured eternal redemption, Hebrews 9:12. The escalation is from a price no one can afford to a price that has been paid. The type falls short only in that the psalm names no payer.

typology.type: God's hand that takes from Sheol, verse 15
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist's confidence is that God will take him, the same verb used of Enoch, Genesis 5:24, and Elijah, 2 Kings 2:11. That receiving is completed in Jesus, who was not abandoned to Sheol or allowed to see decay, as Peter preaches from Psalm 16:10, Acts 2:27-32. Paul calls Him the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and quotes Hosea's taunt against death, 1 Corinthians 15:54-55. The hope of verse 15 becomes a certainty because of His rising. The type is partial in that Enoch and Elijah were taken without dying, while Christ went through death and came out of it, opening the way for the rest.

typology.type: The rich man and his barns, verses 16 to 20
typology.fulfillment: The psalm's warning against admiring the rich who die with nothing finds a portrait in the parable of the rich fool, whose barns were full and whose life was required that night, Luke 12:16-21. In Luke 16 a rich man is buried and finds himself in torment, while a beggar is carried to Abraham's side, Luke 16:22-25. The parables enlarge the psalm by showing the reversal in a story. The correspondence is real but the parables are not the psalm's fulfilment; they are teaching in the same wisdom line, and Jesus adds the note of being rich toward God, Luke 12:21.

typology.type: Death as shepherd versus the LORD as shepherd, verse 14
typology.fulfillment: The psalm has a grim reversal of the shepherd image: the wicked are sheep whose shepherd is Death. The Old Testament's better picture is that of the LORD as the shepherd of His people, Psalms 23:1. Jesus says of Himself, 'I am the good shepherd,' and He lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. Those who hear His voice have eternal life and no one can snatch them from His hand, John 10:27-28. Where Death drives its flock down, the good shepherd goes down first and rises. The type falls short because Death has no rival in the psalm, while in the gospel he has been destroyed, Hebrews 2:14-15.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ first by the problem it states so clearly. Verses 7 and 8 say that no man can redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God, because the redemption of a soul is costly and no payment will ever suffice. In the whole Old Testament there is hardly a plainer statement of the human predicament before death. The gospel does not soften it. It says the psalm is right: no one could pay. And then it announces that someone did. 'For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The Greek word behind 'ransom' in Mark is lutron, the price of release, and the same family of words is used for redemption in Romans 3:24 and Ephesians 1:7. The person the psalm said could not exist is the one Jesus claims to be.

The cost is spelled out. Peter writes that we were not redeemed with perishable things such as silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot, 1 Peter 1:18-19. The psalm's rich cannot pay because they have only silver and gold. Christ pays with His life. The writer to the Hebrews adds that He entered the Most Holy Place by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption, Hebrews 9:12. Notice the word: eternal. Verse 8 said that payment would have to be for ever, and the ransom of Christ is.

It leads to Christ by the hope of verse 15. The psalmist's confidence that God will redeem his life from the hand of Sheol and take him to Himself is what the resurrection turns into fact. Peter reads Psalm 16:10, which uses the same word for 'decay' as verse 9 here, as being fulfilled by the resurrection of Jesus, Acts 2:27-32. Paul says that Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the taunt of Hosea 13:14 against Death and Sheol becomes a song, 1 Corinthians 15:54-55.

It leads to Christ by the reversal of the shepherd image. Death is the shepherd of the proud in verse 14, and the good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. Jesus is also the true wise man, speaking in riddles and parables and telling his hearers to lay up treasure in heaven, Matthew 6:19-21. He asked what a man could give in exchange for his soul, Matthew 16:26, in words that could be a commentary on this psalm.

A caution keeps the link honest. The psalm does not name a Messiah, and its hope may have been held in only partly formed language by the psalmist himself. The New Testament does not quote Psalm 49 as a prophecy of Christ. The connection is thematic and rests on the way the gospel answers exactly the problem the psalm poses, and on the way the New Testament uses the same words, redeem and take, for what God did in Christ.
study.god:
The psalm shows God first as the one who alone can ransom. It is a striking way of speaking about Him. Most of the Old Testament describes God as Redeemer of Israel from Egypt, from enemies, from iniquity, as in Psalms 130:7-8. Here redemption is looked at from the other side. The point is not how much God gives but how much no one else can. Human resources, however great, run out at the edge of the grave, and God's do not. When He redeems, He does what money, power and wisdom cannot.

He is not impressed by wealth. The psalm sets no store by the splendour of houses, the extent of estates or the praise of men. In the view of this psalm, God sees the rich and the poor equally as mortal, and the only advantage is that a person has Him. That is not a threat to the well-off but an equalising: 'rich and poor alike,' verse 2, are addressed as one. God's evaluation of a life, on this psalm, does not depend on possessions.

He is Lord of life and death. The realm of Sheol is not outside His reach. Death is called a shepherd in verse 14, but the psalm makes clear that death is a shepherd only of those who have nothing else, and that God is able to take a person out of its hand. Hannah's song says the LORD brings death and gives life, brings down to Sheol and raises up, 1 Samuel 2:6. This psalm is one of the places where that statement is applied to an individual's hope.

He is faithful to those who trust Him. The confidence in verse 15 is not in the psalmist's merit but in God's own character. He 'will surely take me to Himself,' and the sense is that of a relationship: God wants his people with Him. This is a God who is not only Judge and Redeemer but One who receives.

There is a tension in the psalm that should be named. It is the tension between what is said of all humanity, that we are like the beasts that perish, and what is said of the psalmist, that God will redeem him. The psalm does not resolve this by making the psalmist better. It resolves it by making God the difference.

For worship, the psalm teaches a right kind of poverty. It frees the worshiper from the need to trade on anything he owns. A congregation that has sung this psalm can face the wealthy without envy and the grave without dread, because its security is not held in its own hands. It can also give thanks that the one price that could not be paid was paid for us.

crossReferences.note: An owner liable for a death by his ox may redeem his life by paying what is demanded. It shows the ordinary use of redemption by payment in Israel's law, against which the psalm sets the one case, death itself, where no payment can be enough.

At the census each man pays the LORD a ransom for his life so that no plague comes on the people. The word for ransom is the one in Psalm 49:7, and the text shows that a life was thought to be owed to God and to require a covering.

The psalmist who envied the wicked entered God's sanctuary and discerned their end: slick ground, sudden ruin. It answers the same problem as Psalm 49 by pointing to the end, and its verse 24 shares the hope of being received by God.

God will not abandon the soul to Sheol or let His Holy One see decay, and shows the path of life. The phrase to see decay is the same in Psalm 49:9, and this psalm shares the confidence of Psalm 49:15 that God's people are not left in the grave.
God says He will ransom them from the power of Sheol and redeem them from Death. It uses the redemption vocabulary of Psalm 49:15, and Paul cites its taunt at death in 1 Corinthians 15:55.
As a man came from his mother's womb, so he departs, naked as he arrived, taking nothing for his labor. The wisdom writer says what Psalm 49:17 says in the same spirit: wealth stays behind.

A rich man plans bigger barns and is told his life is required that night. Jesus draws the lesson that this is how it goes for anyone who stores up treasure but is not rich toward God. It is the psalm's warning in a story.

What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul, or what can he give in exchange for it? Jesus asks the question that Psalm 49:7-8 answered with 'nothing that suffices,' and He then goes to the cross to give what is needed.
The Son of Man came to give His life as a ransom for many. It is the answer to the impossibility of Psalm 49:7-9: the payment no man can make is made by the one who is more than a man.

We brought nothing into the world and can take nothing out, and the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Paul applies the psalm's point about wealth and death to the temptations of the Christian community.

Believers were redeemed not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ. The very materials by which the rich in Psalm 49 hoped to buy security are named and set aside in favour of the blood of the Lamb.

When the perishable is clothed with the imperishable, death is swallowed up in victory. Paul gives the fulfilment of the hope in Psalm 49:15: God's redeeming of a life from Sheol is completed in the resurrection body.

study.oneStory:
The psalm answers a question that began in the garden. In Genesis 2:17 the LORD warned that death would come, and in Genesis 3 the man and the woman were sent away from the tree of life. From then on every human being is born under the sentence that the rich man in this psalm cannot escape. The account of Adam's line in Genesis 5 rings with 'and then he died,' with one exception, Enoch, of whom it says God took him, Genesis 5:24. Psalm 49 asks why that is so and whether anything can change it, and it answers first that nothing human can.

It speaks to a question that runs through Israel's story: what is the worth of a life, and who can redeem it? The Passover lamb, the ransom money at the census, the redeeming of the firstborn and the kinsman-redeemer of Ruth all show redemption as a payment made by another. The psalm takes these institutions to their limit and says that at the boundary of death no one can pay. That is what makes verse 15 astonishing. It is the promise that God Himself will be the payer.

The story then moves toward the cross. Isaiah says that the LORD will swallow up death forever and wipe away the tears from every face, Isaiah 25:8. Daniel hears of many who sleep in the dust of the earth waking to everlasting life, Daniel 12:2. In Christ the promise takes flesh. He gives His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45, He is raised as firstfruits, 1 Corinthians 15:20, and those who are His will be raised at His coming, 1 Corinthians 15:23.

The present time is one in which believers still watch the rich prosper and the grave close. The psalm equips them for that: do not fear, do not envy, do not trust in what dies. They live as those who have been redeemed at a price and who wait to be taken.

The new creation is verse 15 fulfilled in every detail. Death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire, Revelation 20:13-14, and God dwells with His people, wiping away every tear, with no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:3-4. The riddle the psalmist sang with the harp is solved, and the ones who were taken to Himself will not need to be afraid again.

quiz.q: Who is this psalm addressed to?

options.text: All peoples, low and high, rich and poor alike, not Israel alone.
options.note: Verses 1-2 explicitly widen the address to all inhabitants of the world.

options.text: Only the wealthy oppressors of Israel.
options.note: The wealthy oppressor is discussed, but the address is universal, not limited to them.

options.text: Only the priests of the temple.
options.note: The psalm names no such restricted audience.

options.text: Only the psalmist's own household.
options.note: The psalm is far broader than a private household; it opens to all inhabitants of the world.

quiz.q: According to verses 7-9, why can no man redeem his brother from death?

options.text: The redemption of a soul is too costly, and no payment can ever suffice.
options.note: This is stated explicitly; the price of a life is beyond any human wealth.

options.text: God has forbidden anyone from trying.
options.note: The text gives the reason as cost, not prohibition.

options.text: Because such ransom money does not exist anywhere.
options.note: The point is not scarcity of money but that no amount can meet the true cost of a life.

options.text: Because brothers are not permitted to help one another.
options.note: The psalm nowhere forbids helping; it says the price of redeeming a soul from death is beyond any human means.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's central turn in verses 14-15?

options.text: From the wicked shepherded by death into Sheol, to the psalmist's hope that God will redeem his life from Sheol.
options.note: This is the hinge of the whole psalm, moving from universal helplessness to personal, God-given hope.

options.text: From poetry into a historical narrative.
options.note: The psalm remains poetic throughout; the shift is in content and hope, not literary form.

options.text: From addressing all peoples to addressing only kings.
options.note: The address does not narrow to kings; the shift is theological, not about audience.

options.text: From describing wealth to describing poverty.
options.note: Wealth and poverty are both mentioned earlier; the decisive shift here is from death's power to God's redeeming power.

quiz.q: What is the psalm's refrain, repeated in verses 12 and 20?

options.text: A man, despite his wealth, without understanding, is like the beasts that perish.
options.note: This refrain brackets the whole psalm and drives home its central point about wealth and mortality.

options.text: Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord.
options.note: True and biblical elsewhere, but not the specific refrain of this psalm.

options.text: The Lord is my shepherd, I shall not want.
options.note: That refrain belongs to Psalm 23, not Psalm 49.

options.text: Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
options.note: A kindred theme to Ecclesiastes, but not this psalm's actual refrain.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament answer the impossible ransom described in this psalm?

options.text: Jesus gives His life as a ransom for many, succeeding where no mere man could, Mark 10:45.
options.note: Christ alone accomplishes the redemption this psalm says is beyond any human being's power.

options.text: By teaching that wealth, rightly used, can eventually purchase eternal life.
options.note: This directly contradicts both the psalm and the gospel; no wealth can purchase eternal life.

options.text: By declaring that death is simply an illusion to be overcome by right thinking.
options.note: Scripture treats death as a real enemy, finally defeated only through Christ's resurrection, not through denial.

options.text: By promising that everyone will eventually redeem themselves through good works.
options.note: This understates the psalm and the gospel; both insist a ransom is beyond human ability to provide for oneself.

questions: This psalm says no amount of wealth can ransom a life from death. Where are you tempted to find security in money or possessions rather than in God?

The psalmist admits he could fear when surrounded by wicked, wealthy oppressors. Where do you find yourself fearing or envying those who prosper through injustice, and how does this psalm reframe that fear?

Verse 15 turns from universal helplessness to personal hope, God will redeem my life from Sheol. How does knowing Christ has already paid the ransom no one else could pay change how you face your own mortality?
The refrain calls a man without understanding, however rich, no better than a beast that perishes. What would it look like this week to actively seek understanding, wisdom that outlasts wealth?
David's hope was that God would take him to Himself beyond the grave. How does the reality of Christ's own resurrection deepen or confirm that same hope for you?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew of this verse is notably difficult, and versions vary in how they render 'their inward thought' or how the lands are named after their owners; the general sense, that death makes a mockery of ambition and legacy, is not in doubt.
Death will be their shepherd renders a striking Hebrew image, reversing the expected picture of a shepherd who protects, since here death itself leads the wicked as a flock down to the grave.
Redeem translates padah, a verb used elsewhere for costly, decisive acts of rescue, such as God redeeming Israel from Egypt; here it describes an even greater rescue, a life from Sheol itself.
